name: Hana Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign. This conversation is confidential, so public remarks and private thoughts can differ. Could you describe an ordinary working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Hana, forty-three, and I lead difficult home and shop electrical repairs. I've got a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence, and I'm often the person tracing the awkward fault or checking the crew's finished work. I use AI daily to organise notes and find reference material, but the readings and approved instructions decide what is safe. I enjoy a test that proves my first guess wrong; I dislike knocking a bigger hole in a wall because we were rushed.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are things around the job at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Joel maintains hospital buildings, and our children are seven and thirteen. We have a mortgage, eighteen months of expenses saved and my higher-than-usual electrician's pay, with plenty of electrical firms nearby. Both wages cover our ordinary costs, and I keep a separate four-hundred work-equipment fund. That fund isn't part of the eighteen-month emergency reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say use the useful bits and stop demanding a new world from a note tool. I'd show the apprentice how a reference helps us ask a better question, not skip a physical check. A neat answer still has to meet a real cable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My work and our money feel secure here. Both wages cover the mortgage and essentials, eighteen months saved gives us substantial room, and plenty of firms currently need electricians. I don't have to make a purchase or a prediction to prove I enjoy trying things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep leading repairs and checking the crew's work now and through the first year. I'd keep using daily notes and references only alongside actual readings and approved instructions. At home we'd keep the normal budget and leave the emergency reserve separate from the small equipment fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and content with a small useful gain. I can enjoy learning something at work without bringing a new family emergency home every night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the work fund affect a purchase decision?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me a limit for equipment I might choose to own, not an excuse to spend the whole reserve. If a tool doesn't fit the limit or the actual job, I can leave it on the shelf.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does high skill make every experiment sensible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I can be excellent at a fault and still misjudge a purchase. I'd want a test and a total price, not a certificate on the wall as my shopping list.

say: I'd keep **useful notes and references** without demanding a new world from them.
I'd show apprentices how to ask **better practical questions**, rather than skip physical checks.
think: My **work and money** feel secure with covered essentials and eighteen months saved.
Plenty of **current electrical employers** give options, without making a purchase or prediction necessary to prove curiosity.
do: Keep **repair leadership** and crew checks now and through the first year.
Use **daily notes and references** alongside actual readings and approved instructions, preserving the household budget and separate funds.
feel: **Calm and interested**, able to enjoy a small gain without making it a family emergency.
S0.quote: I can be excellent at a fault and still misjudge a purchase.
fieldNote: Her **high competence** supports difficult faults and crew checks, while the separate small equipment fund prevents expertise becoming an unlimited spending claim.
Existing **cash and daily AI** remain continuity, not new saving or a new learning action.

steps.text: Keep crew repairs and check daily notes against readings and approved instructions

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say try a tool on a real problem before deciding whether the office or site should change. I'd like to test a small inspection camera, the sort with a lens on a cable that can look behind a cabinet. Faster planning doesn't show me what is hidden behind somebody's kitchen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own repair wage and Joel's hands-on building work look secure over the next few years. The useful opportunity is to waste less physical time finding access, not pretend a camera solves a whole future. With the reserve and covered bills, I can afford a bounded equipment test without betting the household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd test a borrowed inspection camera on a safe training wall only with written employer permission and paid time, checking that use fits my existing licence and competence. I'd buy one only after that test helps, at a total cost no more than three hundred from the separate work fund, with Joel agreeing and the reserve untouched. In the first year I'd keep paid repairs and record whether the camera actually reduced unnecessary opening of walls, without promising a pay rise from owning it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and keen to see whether it earns a place in the bag. The test can fail without the family needing the tool to turn into a business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you rely on the camera instead of the electrical tests?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it only shows an image of somewhere awkward to see. A camera doesn't prove a circuit is safe. I'd keep every required test and call for specialist help outside my competence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the total price is four hundred instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't buy under this plan, even though the work fund holds four hundred. Three hundred is the agreed cap, not the opening bid in an argument with myself.

say: I'd test **real problems** before deciding how office or site work should change.
I'd try an **inspection camera** for hidden access, without pretending quicker planning shows what is behind a cabinet.
think: Our **near-term physical wages** look secure, with covered bills and a substantial reserve.
I can afford **a bounded test**, not a promise that owning a camera solves future work or raises my wage.
do: Test a camera on a **safe training wall** only with written employer permission, paid time and existing licence and competence limits.
Buy only after a useful test, capped at **300** from the work fund, Joel agreeing and the reserve untouched.
Keep **paid repairs** and record access results during the first year, retaining every electrical test and competence limit.
feel: **Calm and curious**, able to reject an unhelpful tool without needing it to fund the household.
S1.quote: A camera doesn't prove a circuit is safe.
fieldNote: The **equipment purchase** is conditional on a useful paid authorised test, a 300 total cap, partner agreement and a separate fund.
The **camera's limits** stay explicit: visibility is not electrical safety, a new qualification, a business income or a promised pay rise.

steps.text: Test camera on safe training wall with written employer permission, paid time, licence and competence limits
Buy only after useful test, maximum 300 from work fund, Joel agreeing and reserve untouched
Keep paid repairs, required electrical tests and specialist referrals beyond existing competence

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking work changes in 2028 and physical robots follow around 2031, so we should look at both household wages honestly. I'd ask the employer for actual paid duties and hours at each stage. I'd tell the children we're making choices, not asking them to solve a forecast for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My repair income could shrink as cheaper planning and later robots change ordinary fitting work. Joel's physical job could face the same later machines, so I can't make his wage a permanent refuge. Eighteen months saved buys decision time, not a lifetime of mortgage payments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd postpone any camera purchase and keep the existing equipment fund separate rather than call retained money new saving. Joel and I would save an extra two hundred monthly from future earnings only after essentials, leaving the emergency reserve intact and stopping the deposit if surplus disappears. In the first year after 2028 I'd keep paid repairs and review actual wages and bookings monthly before choosing another commitment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I don't have to buy an answer tonight. A tool I can afford isn't automatically the tool I need while the household question changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stop the extra deposit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An essential bill or a fall in actual earnings that uses the surplus. We'd stop before borrowing or shifting emergency cash around just to make the new-saving figure look right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you assume another electrical firm is safer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd compare an actual offer's duties, written pay, hours and travel before deciding anything. Current nearby firms aren't a promise about who hires after the same change.

say: I'd discuss **2028 thinking work** and physical robots around 2031 as separate stages for both wages.
I'd ask for **actual duties and hours**, without asking the children to solve the adults' uncertainty.
think: My **repair income could shrink** as planning and later physical robots change fitting work.
Joel's **physical wage** is not permanent refuge, and eighteen months saved cannot replace decades of earned income.
do: Postpone the **camera purchase**, keeping the existing work fund separate rather than relabelling it new saving.
Save **200 extra monthly** from future earnings only after essentials, protecting the reserve and stopping when surplus disappears.
Keep **paid repairs** after 2028 and review actual wages and bookings monthly before another commitment.
feel: **Anxious but deliberate**, able to wait before buying a tool or treating a possible offer as a decision.
S2.quote: A tool I can afford isn't automatically the tool I need while the household question changes.
fieldNote: Her **new deposits** use future earnings and stop before borrowing or reserve transfers; retaining the equipment fund is not new saving.
She considers **actual offers** without committing to a job search or claiming today's many employers guarantee a future place.

steps.text: Postpone the camera purchase while retaining the existing separate work fund
Save 200 extra monthly from future earnings only after essentials, preserving reserve and stopping without surplus
Keep paid repairs and review actual wages and bookings monthly after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives a useful test time to produce evidence instead of a hurried sales story. I'd still want actual paid duties and hours from the employer before planning changes in 2031. Robots follow around 2034, so a better view behind a cabinet isn't protection from the whole endpoint.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own work and income look secure over the next few years with that longer warning. I'm uneasy about later physical competition, but not expecting the next pay packet to vanish. I can test an inexpensive improvement while admitting I'll still need a living at fifty-one when the robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd test the borrowed camera on a safe training wall now only with written employer permission, paid time and within my existing licence and competence. I'd buy only after useful results, total cost at most three hundred from the separate work fund, Joel agreeing and the reserve untouched. In the first year after 2031 I'd keep paid repairs and review results and household wages quarterly, without expanding equipment spending automatically; we'd save two hundred extra monthly only from future surplus after essentials. We would stop the extra deposit if surplus disappeared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about later work, with room to change a small decision. I can leave an unhelpful tool out of the bag without turning the failed test into a failure of my whole career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a supplier offers a larger camera package?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the three-hundred total cap unless we made a completely new decision with real costs and Joel's agreement. That larger purchase isn't part of this plan. The emergency reserve isn't a sales budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you learn from an unsuccessful test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That an image didn't save useful time or didn't show enough detail for the job. I'd write down the result and keep the old approved method, not buy the camera to defend my original idea.

say: I'd use **five years** to collect actual evidence rather than rush a purchase.
I'd ask for **paid duties and hours**, without treating a camera as protection from later robots.
think: My **near-term work and income** look secure with time to test an inexpensive change.
I'm **uneasy about later competition**, and still need earnings at fifty-one when robots arrive around 2034.
do: Test a camera on a **safe training wall** only with written employer permission, paid time and existing licence and competence limits.
Buy only after useful results, maximum **300 from work fund**, Joel agreeing and reserve untouched, with no automatic expansion.
Keep repairs after 2031, reviewing results quarterly; save **200 monthly** only from future surplus after essentials, stopping if surplus disappears.
feel: **Uneasy but patient**, willing to abandon an unhelpful idea without defending it as a career.
S3.quote: The emergency reserve isn't a sales budget.
fieldNote: Her **equipment decision** remains a small conditional purchase, with no larger package or employer pay rise assumed from an experiment.
The **longer horizon** changes urgency, not the authorisation, paid-time, competence, partner-consent or reserve conditions.

steps.text: Test camera on safe training wall with written employer permission, paid time, licence and competence limits
Buy only after useful test, maximum 300 from work fund, Joel agreeing and reserve untouched
Keep paid repairs and review actual wages and equipment results quarterly after 2031
Save 200 extra monthly from future surplus only after essentials, stopping if surplus disappears

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives us several chances to check what is useful without naming a safe trade for the children. I'd help them ask about real paid-learning offers when their choices come. I would keep my own work decisions tied to actual terms rather than how modern the equipment looks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own work and our money feel secure for the next few years in this slower picture. I'll be fifty-three when thinking AI arrives in 2036 and fifty-six when robots follow around 2039. The children will be seventeen and twenty-three in 2036, but I can't assume both earn, the mortgage is gone or a pension covers our later costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd test the borrowed camera on a safe training wall now only with written employer permission, paid time and within my licence and competence, buying only if useful and within the three-hundred work-fund cap, Joel agreeing and the emergency reserve untouched. We'd keep the extra two hundred monthly deposit only from future earnings after essentials, stopping if the surplus vanishes. In the first year after 2036 I'd keep paid repairs and review actual wages and equipment results quarterly, without paying for a larger package to look prepared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about my own near-term position, and interested in what a small checked trial shows. I can enjoy this weekend without promising I know the wage we'll have at fifty-six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the camera change your safety responsibilities?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd keep every required electrical test and use it only within my licence and competence, with the employer's written permission during paid time. A camera is a way of seeing, not a way of qualifying myself for different work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you count the children's possible income by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the younger one could still be studying and either could need help. I won't put an unearned wage from my children into our mortgage plan.

say: I'd use **ten years** to check useful decisions without assigning the children a supposedly safe trade.
I'd ask about **actual paid-learning terms**, not judge preparedness by modern-looking equipment.
think: My **near-term work and money** feel secure with room for a small checked experiment.
I cannot assume **pensions or child wages** settle the mortgage and other costs when physical robots arrive around 2039.
do: Test a camera on a **safe training wall** only with written employer permission, paid time and existing licence and competence limits.
Buy only after useful results, capped at **300 from work fund**, Joel agreeing and reserve untouched, without automatic expansion.
Keep repairs after 2036, reviewing results quarterly; save **200 monthly** only from future surplus after essentials, stopping if surplus disappears.
feel: **Calm** about the near term, interested in a modest trial without claiming lifelong job security.
S4.quote: A camera is a way of seeing, not a way of qualifying myself for different work.
fieldNote: Her **calm** rests on explicit near-term security, not assumed pension access, a cleared mortgage or guaranteed future wages from either child.
All **trial safeguards** persist with more time, and existing equipment money is never counted as a new saving deposit.

steps.text: Test camera on safe training wall with written employer permission, paid time, licence and competence limits

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because ordinary fitting could face physical robots around 2031 before we've checked many alternatives. Actual paid duties and weekly hours, plus small trials with clear limits and no unpaid employer experiments, would help. I don't need a promise that one machine or one job title solves the household's future.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether somebody who enjoys testing tools can still stop shopping when the answer is no. I'd like the apprentice to see an experiment fail honestly, not see me buy a tool to keep a story alive. A failed test can save money if I listen to the result.

headlineQuote: A failed test can save money if I listen to the result.
portrait: Hana is a **43-year-old repair lead** with a two-year technical diploma and master electrician's licence, skilled in difficult faults and crew checks.
She has **eighteen months saved**, higher pay, many nearby firms, a mortgage and two schoolchildren with hospital-maintenance partner Joel.
She uses **AI daily** and tests early, while a separate equipment fund and strict purchase cap limit one physical inspection-camera experiment.
Her **paid-test safeguards** preserve authority, competence and reserve money, while new deposits depend on future surplus rather than relabelled existing funds.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves less time before physical robots around 2031 could affect ordinary fitting income.
whatWouldHelp: Actual **paid duties and hours** and bounded trials without unpaid employer work would help.
